subject: english-language
topicDisplay: Paper 1 Explorations In Creative Reading And Writing
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the assessment objectives.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Words such as "however," "meanwhile" and "firstly" that signal the direction of a text are:
questions.explain: Connectives that guide the reader through a text are discourse markers.

questions.q: A third-person narrator who knows the thoughts and feelings of every character is described as:
questions.explain: An omniscient narrator has access to all characters' inner thoughts and the wider story.

questions.q: What is the reader most likely meant to FEEL from: "The orphan watched the other children open their gifts, his own hands empty"?
questions.explain: The image of the empty-handed orphan beside happy children is designed to evoke sympathy.

questions.q: You are writing a speech. Which feature would make it most engaging for a live audience?
options: A repeated phrase used as a rallying refrain
Long, unbroken paragraphs of dense detail
questions.explain: Repetition (anaphora) builds rhythm and impact, ideal for spoken delivery.

questions.q: Early in a story, a character nervously eyes a loaded gun on the wall. Hinting at a later event is:
questions.explain: Planting an early hint of something to come is foreshadowing.

questions.q: What does 'planning' your writing before you start mainly help you to do?
options: Organise ideas logically and avoid drifting off task
questions.explain: Planning structures ideas in advance so the writing stays coherent and on-task.

questions.q: Which sentence opener creates the most engaging, dramatic story opening?
options: The door slammed shut behind me, and the lights went out.
I am going to tell you about a time I was scared.
It was a normal day at school.
My name is Tom and this is my story.
questions.explain: Starting in the middle of the action (in medias res) hooks the reader immediately.

questions.q: "Her smile was as bright as the sun." This is an example of a:
questions.explain: A comparison using "as" is a simile.

questions.q: An exam asks: "How does the writer use language to create a sense of fear?" What should your answer focus on?
options: Retelling the plot of the extract
Specific words and phrases and the effects they create
questions.explain: A "how does the writer use language" question requires analysis of word choices and their effects, not plot summary.

questions.q: To "zoom in" on the quotation "her hands trembled like leaves in a storm," the strongest analytical move is to:
options: Say it is a nice description
Comment on the simile and what the comparison suggests about her
questions.explain: Zooming in means analysing the chosen technique (a simile) and the specific impression it gives.

questions.q: You are writing a leaflet for a local charity event. Which feature is most appropriate to the form?
options: Clear headings, bullet points and key details like time and place
A single dense block of text
questions.explain: Leaflets use headings, bullets and signposting so readers can scan key information quickly.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a discourse marker such as 'however' or 'furthermore'?
options: To signal the relationship between ideas and guide the reader
questions.explain: Discourse markers connect ideas and show contrast, addition or sequence to aid coherence.
